_comment: The demo's presentation, read by tools/demo_page.html through tools/demo.py. The product comes first with no cables, watched over Bluetooth; then every board is plugged in ('action': 'tether') for the story of how it was built and tested, each claim broken on cue and measured. Every claim is backed by README.md or docs/DECISIONS.md; cite the decision, and change this file when a claim changes. 'say' is what the narrator reads; 'body' is what the screen shows. A chapter with 'demo' runs that scenario live after its narration. 'view' picks what fills the stage: map, hardware, watch (tools/grid_watch.py) or flasher (site/flash). 'media' names the owner's photos or short clips for that chapter, looked for in build/demo-media/ (not in git); one that is not there is not shown. A chapter may give 'lead' and 'points' instead of 'say' and 'body': the title shows alone while the lead is said, then each point appears as its own line is said. 'view': 'diagram' shows the site's own assets/network-diagram.svg; 'focus' on a point, 'lead_focus', or a chapter's 'focuses' (spread over its sentences) zoom it to a named region (FOCUS in the page).

chapters.title: A messaging network you build yourself

points.text: Made from small, inexpensive ESP32 boards.
points.say: It is a messaging network you build yourself, from small, inexpensive boards.

points.text: Access points find each other and form the network on their own.
points.say: A few access points find each other, and form the network on their own. Nobody configures them.

points.text: Touchscreen handhelds send text, alerts and voice across it.
points.say: People carry touchscreen handhelds, and send text, alerts and voice to each other across it.

points.text: No Internet, no phones, no accounts.
points.say: It needs no Internet, no phone, and no account. Everything stays on the network itself.

media.caption: Every handheld model, side by side

chapters.title: Three radios, each with a job

media.caption: The whole grid on one table

chapters.lead: Three radios, each with a job.

points.text: Wi-Fi (ESP-NOW) between access points, and each handheld's link to its access point (D2).
points.say: Wi-Fi carries the everyday traffic: between access points, and from each handheld to its access point.

points.text: LoRa: a second, much longer path between access points, and to handhelds that have a module (D71, D77).
points.say: LoRa is a second, longer path, between access points, and to handhelds that have a module.

points.text: Bluetooth: a laptop or phone watches the grid's health without joining it (D68).
points.say: Bluetooth lets a laptop or a phone watch the network, without ever joining it.

points.text: No master: every access point holds the whole grid's settings, groups and time (D45, D46).
points.say: There is no master. Every access point holds a full copy of the settings, the groups and the time.

points.text: Handhelds spread themselves across access points, and move when one disappears (D54).
points.say: And the handhelds spread themselves across the access points.

chapters.title: Everything here runs on its own batteries

media.caption: Access points on their own power

chapters.lead: First, the product, the way people would use it.

points.text: No cable to any board: access points on batteries or chargers, handhelds on their own batteries.
points.say: There is no cable to any board. The access points run on batteries or chargers, and the handhelds on their own batteries.

points.text: This laptop only listens to the access points' Bluetooth beacons; it cannot send, change or break anything (D68).
points.say: This laptop only listens to a Bluetooth beacon each access point sends. It cannot send, change, or break anything.

points.text: What you see on the map is what the grid says about itself, live.
points.say: So everything on this map is the network describing itself.

chapters.title: An SOS from a handheld's own screen
body: Raise an SOS on any handheld.
Every other screen shows it; pressing Read tells the sender who has seen it (D58).
The sender marks themselves safe, and it is stood down everywhere (D79).
chapters.say: The reason it exists. Somebody needs help. They raise an S O S from their handheld's screen.

media.caption: An SOS on a locked handheld

chapters.part: Live: pull a plug, by hand
chapters.title: Pull the plug on an access point, by hand
body: Unplug any access point you like.
The laptop sees it go quiet over Bluetooth, and sees its handhelds turn up on the others.
Plug it back in, and it rejoins.
chapters.say: Now something goes wrong. An access point loses power. Pull the plug on any one of them.

chapters.title: Every access point off, then on, with no cables
body: Switch every access point off; the handhelds keep the time on their own batteries.
Switch them back on: they find each other, and the handhelds give them the time back (D53).
chapters.say: And the worst case. Every access point goes off at once.

chapters.title: A laptop or a phone watches the grid without joining it
body: Every access point broadcasts a small sealed status over Bluetooth; anyone with the key can read it (D68).
After a login, the same tabs the admin page shows: network, handhelds, traffic (D70).
Read-only by construction: a watcher can never send, change or take part (D69, D70).
Every access point also serves the admin page itself, on request (D45, D91).
chapters.say: You do not have to join the network to see how it is doing. What drew that map is the same view anyone can open: every access point broadcasts a small, sealed status over Bluetooth, and this laptop listens without being part of the grid. There is an Android app that does the same, and it is read only by construction: a watcher can never send a message or change anything.

chapters.title: Tested by breaking it, for hours, unattended
body: A framework kills access points and handhelds at random, cuts their power and switches their radios off, while the handhelds keep messaging each other.
In a 10-hour run: 55 faults injected, 55 recovered, none needing a human. The backbone re-formed in a median of 3.7 s.
It found five bugs code review and unit tests never could, including one that made the self-healing promise untrue.
This demo uses the same engine, with a script instead of a random schedule.
chapters.say: So that is the product. Now, how we know it holds up. The central claim is that it heals itself, so it was tested by attacking it. A framework kills access points and handhelds at random, cuts their power and turns their radios off, for hours, while the handhelds keep messaging each other. In one ten hour run, fifty five faults were injected and all fifty five recovered without a human. It also found five real bugs that code review never could.

chapters.title: Every board on a cable, so each claim can be broken on cue and measured
body: Each board is plugged into this laptop: to cut its power on cue, and to read what it says.
Faults go through the cable and no other way; nothing in the firmware can break the grid on request (D103).
Every message is still sent and received by the handhelds themselves. The laptop never joins the grid (D25).
Each board is restarted as it is plugged in, so every test starts from a known point.
chapters.say: To measure all of this, we plug every board into this laptop. Not because the grid needs it, but so the laptop can cut a board's power on cue and read what each one says about itself. The handhelds still send and receive every message themselves. Plug them in now.

chapters.title: The boards on this bench, as they describe themselves
body: Access points: plain ESP32 boards with a 4 MB flash, an optional LoRa module (Reyax RYLR998, SX1262) and an optional GPS (GT-U7).
Handhelds: off-the-shelf ESP32 and ESP32-S3 display boards with touchscreens, some with a microphone, speaker or LoRa module.
Every module is optional: with no GPS an admin sets the time, and with no LoRa the access points use Wi-Fi alone.
Board facts live in data-only profiles; a new display board is often a profile and a touch check away.
chapters.say: The hardware is deliberately ordinary. The access points are plain E S P 32 development boards. Some carry a LoRa module, and one can carry a GPS for time and location. The handhelds are off-the-shelf touchscreen boards. Several models run it today, on three different chips. Every module is optional. This table is not typed in: each board reported it as it was plugged in.

media.caption: An access point with its LoRa module
The GPS on an access point
A handheld's LoRa module, wired on

chapters.title: What makes it hold together
body: Information is sticky: anything one device learns survives it restarting and is shared, newest version wins (D48).
Self-healing: a device that restarts gets its state back from the ones that stayed up (D53).
One-to-one messages are end-to-end encrypted; access points carry them without being able to read them (D5).
Emergencies go out over Wi-Fi and LoRa at the same time, so an alert never depends on one radio (D74).
Bounded by design: fixed-size tables, no memory taken per message, and a logged result when anything fills up.
chapters.say: A few ideas hold it together. Information is sticky: anything one device learns survives that device restarting, and is shared with its neighbours, with the newest version winning. A device that restarts gets its state back from the ones that stayed up. One-to-one messages are encrypted end to end, so the access points carry them without being able to read them. Emergencies go out over Wi-Fi and LoRa at the same time. And everything is bounded: fixed tables, no memory taken per message, and a defined result when something fills up.

chapters.title: Decided in writing, before the code
body: D1: pure ESP-IDF, no Arduino, for full control of Wi-Fi, ESP-NOW and memory.
D25: everything is tested on the real boards; a laptop never stands in for a device.
D45: no master access point; any one of them can go and the rest carry on.
D55: the handheld screens are drawn by our own small renderer, not a UI library, to leave memory for the radios.
D96, D97: a device holds its grid's keys, and only installs an update signed by the release key it was given.
D103: faults are injected through a cable and no other way; nothing in the firmware can break the grid on request.
chapters.say: Every decision was made in writing first, and there are more than a hundred of them. A few that shaped it. Pure E S P I D F, for full control of the radios. Testing happens on the real boards, never on a laptop pretending to be one. No master access point. The handheld screens are drawn by our own small renderer, to leave memory for the radios. Each device holds its own grid's keys, and only installs updates signed by the release key it was given. And the fault injection you are about to see goes through a cable: there is nothing in the firmware that can break the grid on request.

chapters.title: One screen per person, no phone needed
body: Each person has a handheld with its own name, chosen on the handheld (D50).
Messages to everyone, to a group, or to one person; a mark shows sent, delivered and read (D42).
Battery, screen lock and a screen saver; the firmware it runs is on its status screen (D62, D110).
chapters.say: With the cables in, the laptop can drive each handheld's screen. A closer look at them.

chapters.title: An SOS breaks through every screen
body: Sent from the handheld's own screen; it takes over every other screen, even a locked one (D57).
It goes out over Wi-Fi and LoRa at the same time (D74).
Read is how an alert is dismissed, and the sender sees who has read it (D58).
The sender marks themselves safe, and one message stands it down everywhere (D79).
chapters.say: The S O S again, this time measured: how long it takes to reach each screen, and which radios carried it.

chapters.title: Push to talk, to one person, a group, or everyone
body: Live, half duplex, in 100 ms frames sealed like text (D61).
A compact copy of each talk also crosses LoRa, for handhelds out of Wi-Fi range (D95).
Handhelds without a microphone still listen.
chapters.say: Voice. Push to talk, to one person, a group, or everyone.

chapters.title: Pull the plug on an access point
body: Its handhelds look for another access point and move by themselves (D54).
Messages keep arriving while it is gone.
When it comes back it rejoins with nothing set up again.
chapters.say: Now we start breaking things. We cut the power to the access point carrying the most handhelds.

chapters.title: An access point crashes and restarts
body: Settings, groups and the grid's time come back from its own flash and from the others (D48, D53, D60).
Nothing is typed in again.
chapters.say: A crash is different from a power cut: the access point comes straight back. Watch what it remembers.

chapters.title: Cut the Wi-Fi between access points
body: The access points switch to LoRa, the longer, slower path (D71).
Each LoRa message is acknowledged and sent again until it is (D104).
A message Wi-Fi could not deliver goes to LoRa at once (D105).
chapters.say: Now we take away the Wi-Fi link between every pair of access points.

chapters.title: A handheld walks out of Wi-Fi range
body: A handheld with a LoRa module stays reachable when no access point's Wi-Fi reaches it (D77).
The grid knows it is on LoRa alone and never pretends it is on Wi-Fi (D80).
Messages to it are acknowledged and sent again until they arrive (D109).
chapters.say: LoRa is not only for access points. A handheld with a module can walk out of Wi-Fi range and stay on the grid.

chapters.title: Split the grid in two, then let it meet again
body: Each half carries on by itself.
Changes made on either side carry a version; when the halves meet, the newest wins (D45, D48).
chapters.say: What if the grid splits in two, and someone changes something on one side?

chapters.title: Every access point off at once
body: The handhelds keep the grid's time and carry it back to the access points (D53).
Trails of where people walked survive every device being off (D106).
The grid re-forms by itself.
chapters.say: And the worst case. Every access point loses power at the same moment.

chapters.title: An update that spreads itself
body: Give a signed update to one access point; it reaches the others by itself (D101).
Access points carry handheld updates and hand them to handhelds over the air (D107, D111).
A device installs only an update signed by the release key it was given (D97).
One command withdraws an update from the whole grid.
chapters.say: Updating a network nobody can plug a cable into. A signed update is given to one access point, and the grid does the rest.

chapters.title: Install it from a web page
body: Plug a board in, open the installer page, press Install and choose the port.
Then give it your grid's file: the keys stay on the device, not in the firmware (D96).
No tools to install.
chapters.say: And finally, how anyone gets started. A board is installed from a web page: press install, choose the port, and give it your grid's file. Nothing to install on the computer.

chapters.title: Everything else it does
body: Groups made on the handhelds while the grid runs (D52); names chosen on the handheld (D50).
A GPS gives the grid its time and location; handhelds with one share position, distance and a trail (D63, D65, D99).
Voice notes that cross LoRa (D72, D95); LoRa power that can be turned down (D98).
A small alert and distress unit that shows alerts and raises an SOS (D66).
A self test at every handheld start (D24); the firmware every device runs shown on every screen (D110).
chapters.say: There is more than we have time to break today. Groups made on the handhelds, while the grid runs. A GPS that gives the grid its time and location, and handhelds that share where they are and leave a trail. Voice notes that cross LoRa. A small alert unit that does nothing but show alerts and raise an S O S. And a self test every time a handheld starts.

chapters.title: Text and voice are two applications on it
chapters.lead: One more thing about what this is.

points.text: The network carries typed, sealed messages; text and voice are two of those types.
points.say: Text and voice are not the network. They are two applications that ride on it. Underneath, it carries typed, sealed messages between devices.

points.text: A new kind of message is a documented change to the protocol core, open to anyone.
points.say: A new kind of message is a documented change to the protocol code, and the code is open for anyone to make it.

points.text: Ideas we have not built: sensors, drone telemetry, trackers, gate and door alerts.
points.say: We have not built these, but the same network could carry readings from sensors, telemetry from drones, trackers, or a gate that says it was opened.

points.text: The watcher is one example: the same pattern could watch sensors, or drones.
points.say: And the watcher you saw is one example of an application that only listens. The same pattern could become a sensor watcher, or a drone watcher.

chapters.title: Some places it could be used
chapters.lead: A few places it could be used.

points.text: A group trip that several families share.
points.say: A group trip that several families share.

points.say: An event, or a festival site.

points.say: A training exercise, or a drill.

points.say: Anywhere people spread out, and want a network of their own.

chapters.title: What it is not, yet
body: A prototype: every test so far ran on one workbench, every board in range and on a cable.
Ranges are not measured yet; field tests come next.
No store and forward: a message to someone unreachable is refused and the sender is told (D13).
The handhelds are development boards; purpose-built handhelds and enclosures are still to come.
chapters.say: And to be straight about it. This is a prototype. Every test so far ran on one bench, with every board in range. We have not measured range yet, so we do not claim any. A message to someone who cannot be reached is refused, and the sender is told, rather than held for later. And the handhelds are development boards for now.

chapters.title: Open source, and built in the open
body: GPL-3.0-or-later: firmware, tools and every design document (D76).
github.com/iamankushpandit/LocalGrid
Board ports, testing on your own radios, and the admin page are the best places to start.
chapters.say: LocalGrid is open source, under the G P L, including every design document and decision. It is on GitHub, at i am ankush pandit, slash LocalGrid. If you build one, we would love to hear how far it reaches. Thank you for watching.
